title: Waldensian Trials: 'Synagogue' Enters Witch Vocabulary
description: In the 1420s–1430s, inquisitorial campaigns against Waldensian heretics in the western Alps began producing trial records in which interrogators used the term 'synagogue' (synagoga) for the alleged diabolical gathering — a term that would become standard in describing the witches' sabbath. These Alpine trials, documented in sources like Johannes Fründ's chronicle of Valais (c.1430) and records from Dauphiné and Savoy, describe flying to nocturnal assemblies, renouncing Christ, feasting, and sexual license in terms nearly identical to later witch sabbath accounts. The convergence of Waldensian heresy prosecution with Alpine folk beliefs in nocturnal assemblies was a crucial moment in the crystallization of the witchcraft stereotype.
historiographical_note: L'Estrange Ewen, followed by Richard Kieckhefer in Magic in the Middle Ages (1989) and Michael Bailey in Battling Demons (2003), identified the Alpine Waldensian trials as the site where the composite witchcraft stereotype first crystallized. The use of 'synagogue' — an anti-Semitic term applied to both Jewish gatherings and heretical assemblies — reveals how multiple forms of religious othering were woven into the witch concept.
source_method: Johannes Fründ chronicle; Valais trial records; Dauphiné inquisitorial records; secondary scholarship on early witch trials
